n: During the last week of His life, while Jesus teaches in the temple, a delegation of chief priests, scribes, and elders — representatives of the ruling council — confronts Him.

f.w: the chief priests and the scribes came upon him with the elders
f.g: These three groups made up the Sanhedrin, the Jewish high council.

n: They demand to know His authority. Who gave Him the right to clear the temple and teach there? They control the temple and never authorized Him.
Jesus answers with a question of His own, a common rabbinic way of debating.

f.w: I will also ask you one thing
f.g: Answering a question with a question was a respected teaching method.

n: Was John’s baptism authorized by God or merely human? The answer to this question also answers theirs, since John testified of Jesus.

f.g: John’s whole ministry, of which baptism was the sign.

n: They huddle privately and see the trap: if they say “from heaven,” He’ll ask why they didn’t believe John.
If they say “from men,” the crowd might stone them, since the people firmly believe John was a prophet. They are more concerned with public opinion than with truth.

f.w: they be persuaded that John was a prophet

n: So they claim not to know. Their non-answer exposes that they aren’t really seeking truth.
Since they refuse to answer honestly, Jesus declines to answer them. Those unwilling to accept truth don’t receive more of it.
Jesus tells the people a parable. A man plants a vineyard, rents it to tenant farmers, and leaves for a long time. Isaiah had used the vineyard as a symbol of Israel.
At harvest the owner sends a servant to collect his share. The tenants beat him and send him away with nothing.

f.g: At harvest time, when rent was due in produce.

n: He sends a second servant, who is beaten and humiliated.
A third is wounded and thrown out. These servants represent the prophets God sent to Israel, many of whom were mistreated.
The owner decides to send his beloved son, hoping they will respect him. The phrase “beloved son” echoes the Father’s words at Jesus’ baptism and Transfiguration.
The tenants recognize the heir and plot to kill him, imagining they will keep the vineyard. Jesus is openly describing the leaders’ plot against Him.
They throw him out of the vineyard and kill him. Jesus would be crucified outside Jerusalem’s walls. He then asks what the owner will do.

f.w: cast him out of the vineyard

n: The owner will destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others. The listeners recoil in horror: may it never be!

f.g: Greek mē genoito — “may it never happen!”

n: Jesus looks right at them and quotes Psalm 118: the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The rejected Son becomes the foundation of everything.

f.w: The stone which the builders rejected

f.g: The cornerstone or capstone — the most important stone in a building.

n: Stumbling over this stone breaks a person; having it fall on them crushes them. Rejecting Christ is ultimately self-destructive.
The leaders realize the parable is about them and want to arrest Him immediately, but they fear the crowd.
They send spies pretending to be sincere, hoping to catch Him in words they could use to hand Him over to the Roman governor.
They begin with flattery: Teacher, You are honest and impartial and teach God’s way truthfully. Their compliments are true, but they don’t mean them.

f.w: acceptest thou the person of any
f.g: Show favoritism based on someone’s status.

n: Then the trap: should we pay taxes to Caesar? Saying yes would anger Jewish patriots; saying no would be treason against Rome.

f.g: A poll tax paid directly to Rome, deeply resented by many Jews.
The Roman emperor, at this time Tiberius.

n: Jesus sees right through their scheme.
He asks for a coin and asks whose image and inscription it bears. They answer: Caesar’s.

f.g: A denarius, a silver coin worth a day’s wage, stamped with the emperor’s portrait.

n: Give Caesar what bears his image, and give God what bears His image — ourselves. We have civil duties, but our whole selves belong to God.

f.w: unto God the things which be God's

n: They couldn’t trap Him publicly. Amazed at His answer, they fall silent.
Next come Sadducees, the priestly aristocratic party who denied the resurrection and accepted only the five books of Moses as authoritative.

f.g: A priestly party that rejected resurrection, angels, and spirits.

n: They cite the law of levirate marriage: if a man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow and raise children in his name.

f.w: raise up seed unto his brother

n: They pose an absurd hypothetical: seven brothers. The first marries and dies childless.

f.g: An exaggerated scenario designed to ridicule belief in resurrection.

n: The second marries her and dies without children.
Then the third, and so on through all seven, none leaving children.
Finally the woman dies too.
Their punchline: in the resurrection, whose wife will she be? They think the question makes resurrection look ridiculous.

f.g: They don’t believe in it; they are mocking the idea.

n: Jesus answers that people of this world marry and are given in marriage. Latter-day revelation teaches that marriages performed only by earthly authority end at death.

Those found worthy of the resurrection don’t marry there. Latter-day Saints understand this to mean marriages are not performed after the resurrection; eternal marriage must be sealed by proper authority beforehand.

f.w: neither marry, nor are given in marriage

n: Resurrected people can never die again. They are like the angels in this respect, and are God’s children, raised to immortal life.

f.w: Neither can they die any more

f.g: Those who share in the resurrection.

n: Jesus proves the resurrection from Moses himself — the very books the Sadducees accepted. At the burning bush, God calls Himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
God isn’t the God of the dead but of the living. If He is still their God, then Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob still live to Him and will rise.
Some scribes — probably Pharisees, who believed in resurrection — compliment His answer.

f.g: Pharisees shared Jesus’ belief in resurrection and enjoyed seeing the Sadducees silenced.

n: After this, no one dares ask Him any more questions.
Now Jesus asks them a question: why do people say the Messiah is merely David’s son?

f.g: A common title for the Messiah, a descendant of David.

n: In Psalm 110, David writes that the LORD (God) said to “my Lord” (the Messiah): sit at My right hand. In Latter-day Saint understanding, this pictures the Father and the Son.

f.w: The LORD said unto my Lord

n: ...until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet — an image of total victory.

f.g: Conquerors sometimes placed their feet on defeated enemies’ necks.

n: If David calls the Messiah “Lord,” how can he be just David’s son? The Messiah must be more than a human descendant — He is David’s Lord, the Son of God.

f.w: how is he then his son?

n: With everyone listening, Jesus warns His disciples.

f.w: in the audience of all the people

n: Watch out for the scribes who love flowing robes, public greetings, and the best seats at synagogues and banquets. Religious status had become their reward.

f.g: Distinguished garments marking them as scholars.
Places of honor at a meal.

n: They exploit widows — perhaps as trustees of their estates — while showing off with long prayers. Those who use religion to exploit the vulnerable will face harsher judgment.
